thm-local-leading-eigenvector-stability-:
## Statement

Let $p\ge2$, let $A\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ be symmetric, and order its
eigenvalues as $\lambda_1(A)\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_p(A)$. Suppose its leading
eigenvalue is simple, with gap
$$
g:=\lambda_1(A)-\lambda_2(A)>0,
$$
and let $v$ be a unit leading eigenvector. Let $E\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$ be
symmetric, put $\epsilon:=\|E\|_{\mathrm{op}}$, and assume
$0\le\epsilon<g/2$. If $\widetilde v$ is any unit leading eigenvector of
$A+E$, then the leading eigenvalue of $A+E$ is simple and
$$ |\lambda_1(A+E)-\lambda_1(A)|\le\epsilon,\qquad \sin\angle(v,\widetilde v):=\sqrt{1-(v^{\mathsf T}\widetilde v)^2}\le\frac{\epsilon}{g-\epsilon}. $$
The bound concerns the line spanned by the eigenvector, so it is unchanged by
either sign choice. It is a local eigengap bound; it does not assert a
dimension-free Davis--Kahan theorem or a finite-sample inference procedure.
thm-sample-centered-covariance-root-n-fr:
## Statement

Fix $p\ge1$ and a Borel probability law $P$ on $\mathbb R^p$ with
$\mathbb E_P\|X\|_2^4<\infty$, mean $\mu$, and covariance matrix $\Sigma$.
For each $n\ge1$, let $X_{n,1},\ldots,X_{n,n}$ be iid with law $P$; the
probability space may depend on $n$. Put
$$ \bar X_n:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_{n,i},\qquad \widehat\Sigma_n^\ast:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(X_{n,i}-\bar X_n)(X_{n,i}-\bar X_n)^{\mathsf T}, $$
the sample-centered covariance with divisor $n$ from
[[def-sample-covariance-and-operator-norm-loss]]. For a matrix $B$, define
$\|B\|_F:=(\sum_{j,k=1}^pB_{jk}^2)^{1/2}$. Then
$$
\|\widehat\Sigma_n^\ast-\Sigma\|_F=O_P(n^{-1/2}),
$$
meaning $\sqrt n\|\widehat\Sigma_n^\ast-\Sigma\|_F=O_P(1)$ in the
bounded-in-probability sense of
[[def-op-and-little-op-stochastic-bounds]]. No Gaussian assumption is needed.
def-covariance-and-correlation-principal:
## Definition

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a parametric statistical model, let $p\ge1$, and let
$X:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^p$ be a measurable random vector with
$\mathbb E_\theta\|X\|_2^2<\infty$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$. Write
$\mu_\theta=\mathbb E_\theta X$ and
$\Sigma_\theta=\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(X)$ as in
[[def-covariance-matrix-of-a-random-vector]]. The map
$\psi(\theta)=\Sigma_\theta$ is the covariance-matrix estimand on this model
([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).

For each $\theta$, list the real eigenvalues of $\Sigma_\theta$ in
nonincreasing order and counting multiplicity. The **covariance-PCA
decomposition** is the list of eigenspaces of $\Sigma_\theta$, ordered by
their distinct eigenvalues from largest to smallest. Equivalently, for each
distinct eigenvalue $\lambda$, its component subspace is
$\ker(\Sigma_\theta-\lambda I)$. The top eigenspace is the leading principal
subspace; when its eigenvalue is simple it is a line, and either unit
representative has the same sign-free direction.
The well-definedness result
[[lem-finite-second-moment-covariance-matrix-is-well-defined]] ensures these
covariance matrices are finite, symmetric, and positive semidefinite. The
real spectral theorem
[[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]] ensures their
eigenspaces span $\mathbb R^p$.

If every coordinate variance $(\Sigma_\theta)_{jj}$ is positive, put
$D_\theta=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{(\Sigma_\theta)_{11}},\ldots,
\sqrt{(\Sigma_\theta)_{pp}})$ and standardize the centered vector as
$Z_\theta=D_\theta^{-1}(X-\mu_\theta)$. Its covariance is the correlation
matrix
$R_\theta=D_\theta^{-1}\Sigma_\theta D_\theta^{-1}$. **Correlation-PCA** is
the ordered eigenspace decomposition of $R_\theta$. Thus both population
conventions center first; correlation-PCA additionally divides each
coordinate by its positive population standard deviation.

For an iid sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, **sample covariance-PCA** uses the
eigenspaces of the sample-centered covariance
$\widehat\Sigma_n^\ast=n^{-1}\sum_i(X_i-\bar X)(X_i-\bar X)^{\mathsf T}$
from [[def-sample-covariance-and-operator-norm-loss]], where
$\bar X=n^{-1}\sum_iX_i$. Sample correlation-PCA standardizes by the
positive sample standard deviations when all sample coordinate variances are
positive. The divisor convention here is $n$, not $n-1$. The sample
covariance matrix is a statistic, and it is an estimator of the covariance
target in its sample experiment, as proved in
[[lem-pca-sample-covariance-is-a-measurable-estimator]].

This definition specifies mathematical matrices under an assumed law. The
scientific model contract distinguishes that assumption from evidence that an
empirical law is adequate; PCA itself makes no such adequacy claim
([[def-scientific-statistical-model-contract]]).
lem-pca-sample-covariance-is-a-measurabl:
## Statement

In an iid sample experiment on Borel data space $(\mathbb R^p)^n$, let the
target be the covariance-matrix estimand $\psi(\theta)=\Sigma_\theta$ of
[[def-covariance-and-correlation-principal-component-analysis]]. For $n\ge1$,
the sample-centered covariance map
$$ T_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n):=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)(x_i-\bar x)^{\mathsf T},\qquad \bar x=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nx_i, $$
is a statistic with target the Borel space of real symmetric $p\times p$
matrices, and hence is an estimator of $\psi$ in the sense of
[[def-statistic-and-estimator]]. This statement asserts measurability and
target type only; it asserts no unbiasedness or consistency.
thm-pca-leading-direction-maximizes-vari:
## Statement

Fix a parameter $\theta$ in the model of
[[def-covariance-and-correlation-principal-component-analysis]], and let
$X$ have finite second moment and covariance matrix $\Sigma_\theta$. For
every unit vector $a\in\mathbb R^p$,
$$ \operatorname{Var}_\theta(a^{\mathsf T}X)=a^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_\theta a. $$
Consequently, the maximum projected variance is the largest eigenvalue
$\lambda_1(\Sigma_\theta)$, and its maximizing unit vectors are exactly the
unit vectors in the leading eigenspace. When all coordinate variances are
positive, the same assertion applied to
$D_\theta^{-1}(X-\mu_\theta)$ says that correlation-PCA maximizes the
variance of linear scores of the standardized coordinates.
thm-repeated-leading-eigenvalue-identifi:
## Statement

Let $\Sigma$ be a covariance matrix in the PCA definition of
[[def-covariance-and-correlation-principal-component-analysis]], with ordered
eigenvalues $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots$. If
$\lambda_1=\lambda_2$, then the leading eigenspace
$E_1=\ker(\Sigma-\lambda_1 I)$ is a uniquely specified subspace of dimension
at least two. Every unit vector in $E_1$ is a leading principal direction,
so the covariance matrix determines this subspace but does not single out a
unit vector in it.
cor-pca-sample-leading-eigenspace-root-n:
## Statement

Let $X_{n,1},\ldots,X_{n,n}$ be iid copies of a fixed
$X\in\mathbb R^p$ with $\mathbb E\|X\|_2^4<\infty$, where $p\ge2$, and let
$\Sigma=\operatorname{Cov}(X)$ have a simple leading eigenvalue with gap
$g=\lambda_1(\Sigma)-\lambda_2(\Sigma)>0$. Let $\widehat\Sigma_n^\ast$ be
the sample-centered covariance with divisor $n$, and put
$\epsilon_n=\|\widehat\Sigma_n^\ast-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ and
$G_n=\{\epsilon_n<g/2\}$. Then $\mathbb P(G_n)\to1$. On $G_n$ the sample
leading eigenspace is a line; define $Z_n$ to be the sine of its angle to the
population leading line and set $Z_n=0$ off $G_n$. Then
$Z_n=O_P(n^{-1/2})$, hence $Z_n\to0$ in probability. In particular, the
sample leading eigenspace is a unique line with probability tending to one.
The angle is line-based and sign-invariant. This is a local
eigenspace-consistency result, not finite-sample inference for a selected
component.
